questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Effects of the Horizontal Scaling on Coefficients
questions.problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x\in R.$
Select the correct options in the reasoning below.The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡({{field-1}})+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡({{field-2}}).
$$

The $3$rd sine coefficient of the series is

$$
{b}_{3}={{field-3}}.
$$

Given that $F(x)={x}^{5}$ and $L=4,$ the $3$rd sine coefficient becomes

$$
{b}_{3}={{field-4}}\,\cdot \,{{field-5}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k\ne 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\frac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)
$$

must have a period of $2L\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}=2\pi .$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)
$$

Therefore, $3$rd sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=4$ and $f(x)={x}^{5},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {\int }_{-4}^{4}{x}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)

$$
g(s)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns),

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\frac{\pi }{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s)=f(\frac{L}{\pi }s),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x):$

$$

questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$

Let $F(x)=6{x}^{2}+5x+1$ for $x\in [-1,1).$ The Fourier series of the $2$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${a}_{0}.$

${a}_{0}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
{a}_{0}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=1$ and $f(x)=6{x}^{2}+5x+1$ for $x\in [-1,1).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(6{x}^{2}+5x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}+x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(2+\frac{5}{2}+1)-((-2)+\frac{5}{2}+(-1)) \\  & =\frac{11}{2}-(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n}{3}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n}{3}x)
$$

Let $F(x)=-3x+1$ for $x\in [-3\pi ,3\pi ).$ The Fourier series of the $6\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${a}_{4}.$

${a}_{4}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=3\pi $ and $f(x)=-3x+1$ for $x\in [-3\pi ,3\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{3\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(-3x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3\pi }x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(-3x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4}{3}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-3x+1\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4}{3}x)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4}{3}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{3\pi }(uv\,{|}_{-3\pi }^{3\pi }-{\int }_{-3\pi }^{3\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\pi }(\frac{3}{4}{[(-3x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4}{3}x)]}_{-3\pi }^{3\pi }-{\int }_{-3\pi }^{3\pi }\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4}{3}x)\cdot (-3)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\pi }(\frac{3}{4}[(-9\pi +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-(9\pi +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4\pi )]+\frac{9}{4}{\int }_{-3\pi }^{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4}{3}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(\frac{1}{4}\cdot 0+\frac{9}{4}\cdot (-\frac{3}{4}){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4}{3}x)]}_{-3\pi }^{3\pi }) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(-\frac{27}{16}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-4\pi )]) \\  & =-\frac{27}{16\pi }(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $F(x)=-5x+2$ for $x\in [-4,4).$ The Fourier series of the $8$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of ${b}_{3}.$

${b}_{3}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the sine coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=4$ and $f(x)=-5x+2$ for $x\in [-4,4).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{3}=\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-4}^{4}(-5x+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-5x+2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-5 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{4}{3\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{3} & =\frac{1}{4}(uv\,{|}_{-4}^{4}-{\int }_{-4}^{4}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{4}{3\pi }{[(-5x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x)]}_{-4}^{4}-{\int }_{-4}^{4}(-\frac{4}{3\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x))(-5)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{4}{3\pi }{[(-5x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x)]}_{-4}^{4}-\frac{20}{3\pi }{\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{4}{3\pi }((-18)(-1)-(22)(-1))-\frac{80}{9{\pi }^{2}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-\frac{4}{3\pi }\cdot 40) \\  & =-\frac{40}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, $L=2.$ Also, $f(x)=2$ for $x\in (0,2)$ and $f(x)=-1$ for $x\in (-2,0).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{0}(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3\pi }{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)]}_{-2}^{0}+\frac{2}{3\pi }{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3\pi ))+\frac{2}{3\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Computing the Coefficients For the Fourier Series

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Effects of the Horizontal Scaling on Coefficients
canonical_examples.problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the $2L$-periodic extension of a function $F(x)$ from $x\in [-L,L)$ to $x \in \mathbb R.$ 
Given that $L=2$ and $f(x) = \cosh{(x+1)}$, find the $4$th cosine and the $4$th sine coefficients.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that multiplying the argument of a function by $k \neq 0$ represents the horizontal stretching of the corresponding graph by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{k}.$

Now, let $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x.$ Then, since $f(x)$ has a period of $2L,$ the function

$$
g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right)
$$

must have a period of $2L \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{L} = 2\pi.$ 

The Fourier series of $g(s)$ is

$$
g(s) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos(ns)+b_n\sin(ns),
$$

where:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ {a}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1 \\ {b}_{n} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(ns)\,\text{d}s,\,n\ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $s=\dfrac{\pi}{L}x$ and using the fact that $g(s) = f\left(\dfrac{L}{\pi}s\right),$ we get the Fourier series of $f(x){:}$

$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
a_n\cos\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)+
b_n\sin\bigg(\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x}\bigg)
$$

Therefore, $4$th cosine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, $4$th sine coefficient of $f(x)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(\frac{L}{\pi }s)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4s)\,\text{d}s \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(\frac{L}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}(\frac{\pi }{L}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{L}{\int }_{-L}^{L}f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{L}x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $L=2$ and $f(x)=\cosh(x+1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x, \\ {b}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Constant Term For the Fourier Series
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{2}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{2}x\right)
$$

Let $F(x)=3x^2-4x+1$ for $x\in[-2,2).$ The Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of $a_0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the constant term is given by

$$
a_0=\frac{1}{L}\int_{-L}^{L} f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=3x^2-4x+1$ for $x \in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(3{x}^{2}-4x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({2}^{3}-2\cdot {2}^{2}+2)-((-2)^{3}-2\cdot (-2)^{2}+(-2))) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2-(-18)) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Coefficients For the Fourier Series
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{2}x\right)+b_n\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{2}x\right)
$$

Let $F(x)=-5x+4$ for $x\in[-2,2).$ The Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the exact value of $a_3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For the Fourier series of a $2L$-periodic function, the cosine coefficients are given by

$$
a_n=\frac{1}{L}\int_{-L}^{L} f(x)\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{L}x\right)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $L=2$ and $f(x)=-5x+4$ for $x \in [-2,2).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
a_3 = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{2} (-5x+4)\cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}x\right)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-5x+4\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-5 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\, & ⇒\,v=\frac{2}{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}(uv\,{|}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3\pi }{[(-5x+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)]}_{-2}^{2}-{\int }_{-2}^{2}\frac{2}{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\cdot (-5)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3\pi }[(-5(2)+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )-(-5(-2)+4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3\pi )]+\frac{10}{3\pi }{\int }_{-2}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2}{3\pi }\cdot 0+\frac{10}{3\pi }\cdot (-\frac{2}{3\pi }){[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}x)]}_{-2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{20}{9{\pi }^{2}}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3\pi )]) \\  & =-\frac{10}{9{\pi }^{2}}(-1-(-1)) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
